newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan car exports spurt but trend still down.
newsitem.headline: Japan car exports spurt but trend still down.

text.p: Japan's car exports surged in October as the yen remained weak, but the industry still expects export volume for the full year to keep falling as the country's automakers produce cars at a brisk pace overseas.
Car industry data released Thursday showed that Japan's vehicle exports rose a hefty 17.6 percent in October from a year earlier to 322,022 units, the fifth straight month of increase.
Exports to the United States rose even more steeply than that, heralding a possible revival of trade friction between the two economic giants.

The Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association (JAMA), which compiled the figures, said the exchange rate was the driving force behind the rise. A strong yen at this time last year depressed car exports while its relative weakness this year has made Japanese cars more competitive overseas.

"October exports rose because of the weaker yen and lower exports last year," a JAMA official said. But the organisation said the total of vehicle exports for 1996 was likely to come in below last year's figure.

Car exports fell a steep 24.2 percent year-on-year in October 1995 as the high yen blunted the competitiveness of Japanese exporters. The yen now stands at around 113 yen to the dollar, against around 101 yen last year.

"Exports will show gains in November and December but Japan's overall vehicle exports in 1996 are bound to fall short of the actual 3.79 million units exported in 1995," the car industry official said.
Japan's car exports in the first 10 months totalled 3.06 million units, down 3.9 percent from the same period in 1995.

The 1995 figure of 3.79 million units was a 15 percent drop from the previous year and marked the 10th year of decline. This relects an exodus of Japanese manufacturing overseas to take production closer to the customer and to mitigate the impact of the stronger yen.
Exports to the United States rose for the second straight month in October, spurting 35.9 percent to 103,098.

Earlier this month Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers' Association (AAMA), said in Tokyo that the weaker yen would increase Japan's exports, reversing progress made in reducing Japan's trade surplus.

On the same day, Japan announced a jump of more than 30 percent in its contentious trade surplus with the United States -- the first increase in 20 months -- as Japanese carmakers took advantage of the weaker yen to export more vehicles.

The JAMA official said the surge in exports to the United States was a reaction to low shipments last year and inventory adjustments. For the year as a whole, car exports to the United States are likely to fall short of the 1.23 million units shipped in 1995, he said.
Japan's auto exports to the United States totalled about 900,000 in January to October, down 15 percent year on year.

After their aggressive push to set up overseas factories, Japanese automakers now manufacture more cars overseas than they export from Japan, producing 4.65 million units overseas last year against 3.79 million exported from Japan.
